title: How to Sleep with Braids and Keep Them Neat
hero_alt: A man with braids asleep on a white pillow
card_text: A durag or silk cover, a light touch of oil on the scalp, no heavy product. How to keep braids neat through the night.
lede: To sleep with braids and keep them neat, cover them with a durag, a silk or satin scarf, or a satin cap, or sleep on a silk or satin pillowcase. Smooth fabric lets the braids slide instead of rub, and rubbing is what causes most of the frizz and lifted hairs you see in the morning. Keep the scalp comfortable with a light touch of oil if it feels dry, and skip heavy products that build up between the rows.
Here's why nights are hard on braids, how to cover them, and the general care that keeps a set looking fresh.

blocks.heading: Friction is the enemy.
paragraphs: Every time you turn your head at night, your braids drag across the pillow. Cotton is rough at that scale. It roughs up the surface of the hair, pulls small hairs loose from the rows, and soaks up moisture.
One night doesn't do much. A week of nights shows up as frizz along the parts and fuzzy edges, which is usually what makes a set look older than it is.
Moisture matters as well. Braids leave more of the scalp exposed, and dry hair along the rows is more likely to break and frizz.

blocks.heading: Durag, scarf or cap.

subsections.heading: Durag
paragraphs: Ties around the head and lays the braids flat. Tie it snug enough to stay put, but not so tight that it marks your forehead or pulls at the edges.

subsections.heading: Silk or satin scarf
paragraphs: Wraps the whole head. Handy for longer braids that need to be folded or tucked up.

subsections.heading: Satin cap
paragraphs: Easy to pull on and off. Works well for shorter sets.

subsections.heading: Silk or satin pillowcase
paragraphs: A backup, or a second layer for nights when the covering slips off.
Whichever you choose, use it every night, not only while the braids are fresh. A covering does the most good in the weeks when the set is already starting to loosen.

blocks.heading: Light, not heavy.
paragraphs: Braids leave lines of scalp exposed, and in a dry climate those lines can feel tight or itchy. A small amount of light oil worked into the parts is a common way to keep the scalp comfortable.
Apply oil to the scalp with your fingertips or a dropper, not by pouring it over the braids. A little goes much further than you'd expect.
Heavy creams, gels and butters tend to sit on the scalp and collect between the rows. Over time that buildup looks like flakes and makes the itch worse, not better.
If your scalp is sore, inflamed or flaking a lot, have a doctor take a look.

blocks.heading: Reset in a minute.
paragraphs: A good night does most of the work, but the first minute of the morning still counts:
bullets: Smooth the edges with your palm instead of pulling at loose hairs.
Leave the rows alone. Picking at frizz lifts more of it.
If the covering was tight, give your scalp a gentle rub with your fingertips, not your nails.
Check the edges and the nape, where coverings slip and friction is worst.

blocks.heading: Nothing lasts forever.
paragraphs: Covering braids slows the wear down. It doesn't stop it. As hair grows, the base loosens and the parts fill in, and at that point the set is ready to come out, however careful you've been.
Pricing changes with the style, which is why Booksy shows braids as {{price:braids}}. Plan on {{minutes:braids}} for the appointment, and text a photo of the look you want to {{phone}} first.

items.q: How do I sleep with braids so they don't frizz?
items.a: Cover them with a durag, a silk or satin scarf or cap, or sleep on a silk or satin pillowcase.

items.q: Should I wear a durag with braids?
items.a: It's a common choice. It lays the braids flat and keeps them off the pillow.

items.q: Should I oil my scalp with braids?
items.a: A little light oil on dry parts is common. Heavy products tend to build up.
It depends on the style and how they're cared for.
